title: How to Talk to Your CAS Coordinator About a…
summary: Learn how to discuss a struggling CAS project with your coordinator, prepare evidence, propose realistic changes, and recover during the fall term.
body_markdown:
If you need to **talk to your CAS coordinator about a struggling project** , act before the problem becomes a deadline crisis. Bring an honest account, evidence of completed work, and one or two realistic proposals. Your coordinator can clarify requirements and help you make responsible changes.


This is particularly useful during the **IB CAS fall term** , when academic demands are increasing but there is usually time to revise an unworkable plan, repair collaboration, or obtain approval for a replacement.


### Understand what your coordinator must determine


CAS is **not awarded a numerical grade** , but it must be completed for the Diploma Programme. The[IB overview of creativity, activity, service](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/) explains that students provide evidence of achieving the seven CAS learning outcomes through their experiences and reflections.


The[official IB CAS project guidance](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/cas-projects/) describes purposeful activity involving planning, progress review, and reflection. The CAS subject brief identifies the required project as a **collaborative series of sequential CAS experiences lasting at least one month** .


Your coordinator therefore needs to decide whether the difficulty is:


- a manageable challenge within a viable project;
- a planning or documentation problem;
- a collaboration, safety, safeguarding, or ethical concern;
- or evidence that the project is no longer workable.


Schools may set their own portfolio platforms, approval forms, supervisor procedures, and internal deadlines. These are not necessarily universal IB rules, but you must follow them because your school confirms CAS completion.


### Prepare evidence before the meeting


Create a one-page project snapshot rather than arriving with only the statement, “My project is failing.” Include:


- the original aim and relevant CAS strands;
- collaborators and their current roles;
- completed actions and remaining tasks;
- the obstacle and when it began;
- supporting schedules, drafts, messages, attendance records, or feedback;
- the effect on participants, safety, or the community;
- two realistic recovery options.


Audit your portfolio as well. The distinction between a project and an ordinary experience matters, so review the[CAS project versus experience explanation](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-counts-as-a-cas-project-vs-a-cas-experience) if your proposed revision might change the project’s status.


Be accurate rather than defensive. Admit missed meetings, unrealistic budgeting, or unclear role allocation when relevant. Document circumstances outside your control, but do not exaggerate them or remove your own responsibility.


### Open the conversation directly


A clear opening shows that you understand the problem and want a usable decision:


> I’m concerned that my CAS project is no longer following the approved plan. We completed the initial planning, but participation has fallen and our November target is unrealistic. I have brought the timeline, current evidence, and two possible revisions. Could you help me determine which option still meets our school’s CAS expectations?


Then explain the situation through facts, impact, and response.


Element What to explain


**Facts** What happened, when it happened, and what evidence supports your account


**Impact** How it affects the aim, collaborators, community, safety, timeline, or evidence


**Response** What you tried already and what you propose next


Avoid saying only that your group is unmotivated. State, for example, that two of five members attended the last three sessions, identify the unfinished tasks, and show how you attempted to reorganize responsibilities.


### Ask questions that produce a clear decision


Before leaving, ask:


- Does the revised plan still qualify as a collaborative CAS project?
- Can we reduce its scale while preserving its purpose?
- Which completed work can remain in my portfolio?
- Does changing a community partner require approval?
- What evidence should I collect next?
- What is the next school checkpoint?


Ask whether each instruction is an **IB requirement** or a **school procedure** . For example, the IB does not prescribe one universal number of reflections, although schools may require entries at designated checkpoints. The[CAS verification overview](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-does-cas-get-verified-in-the-ib-system-official-process-explained) explains why accurate local documentation matters.


### Choose an appropriate recovery option


Reducing the scale is often more responsible than abandoning the original purpose.


Problem Possible response


Too few participants Run fewer sessions for a confirmed group


Inactive collaborators Reassign roles or establish written commitments


Partner withdraws Request approval for another suitable partner


Excessive costs Use borrowed, donated, or digital resources


Unrealistic timeline Extend the schedule or reduce the output


Safety concern Pause immediately and consult a responsible adult


Do not quietly convert the required collaborative project into a solo activity. Do not continue service that ignores consent, dignity, safety, or the community’s stated needs merely because you have invested time.


If discontinuation is necessary, ask what completed work may remain as evidence of investigation, planning, action, and learning. Never present an incomplete project as completed, and remember that you must still undertake at least one qualifying CAS project.


### Reflect on the difficulty honestly


A struggling project can support learning about planning, perseverance, collaboration, personal growth, and ethical choices. Difficulty alone, however, does not prove that a learning outcome has been achieved.


Identify the assumption that proved wrong, how your actions affected others, which feedback changed your thinking, and what you would do differently. The guide to[what CAS coordinators want in reflections](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-cas-reflections-what-coordinators-want) provides a practical structure. If documentation is behind, follow the advice on[recovering from missing CAS reflections](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-happens-if-you-don-t-submit-a-cas-reflection) , but never invent dates, participation, or evidence.


### Use a short recovery schedule


- **Within 48 hours:** contact the coordinator and organize existing evidence.
- **Within one week:** meet, record the decision, and obtain necessary approval.
- **By the next session:** communicate revised roles and deadlines.
- **Every week:** complete an action checkpoint and portfolio update.
- **Before late November:** confirm that the revised plan remains viable.


After the meeting, email a brief summary of what was agreed. This creates a reliable record of the approved recovery plan.


### Conclusion


Speak to your CAS coordinator as soon as you can explain the problem clearly. Bring evidence, accept your share of responsibility, suggest realistic alternatives, and leave with a documented decision. A project can often be repaired, while a discontinued attempt can still produce legitimate reflection if your portfolio remains truthful.


RevisionDojo’s[CAS documentation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/using-revisiondojo-to-strengthen-ib-cas-reflection-and-documentation) and Jojo AI can help you organize reflection questions and recovery checklists. Keep all final reflections accurate and in your own voice.
